entities.name: The Early Modern Science Corpus
entities.label: Text
entities.summary: The Early Modern Science Corpus encompasses the foundational texts of the Scientific Revolution (c. 1543–1750) — the period when European thinkers overturned the ancient and medieval understanding of nature and created modern experimental science. This is arguably the most consequential intellectual transformation in human history, as its methods and discoveries became the engine of the modern world. The corpus is anchored by a sequence of revolutionary works: Nicolaus Copernicus's De Revolutionibus Orbium Coelestium (1543) — proposing the heliocentric model of the solar system, overturning 1,400 years of Ptolemaic geocentrism; Andreas Vesalius's De Humani Corporis Fabrica (1543) — the first accurate anatomical atlas based on human dissection, overturning Galen; Johannes Kepler's Astronomia Nova (1609) — discovering the elliptical orbits of planets; Galileo Galilei's Dialogo sopra i Due Massimi Sistemi del Mondo (1632) — the devastating case for heliocentrism that provoked his trial by the Inquisition; William Harvey's De Motu Cordis (1628) — discovering the circulation of blood; René Descartes's Discours de la Méthode (1637) and Principia Philosophiae (1644) — establishing the mechanistic philosophy and mathematical method; Robert Boyle's The Sceptical Chymist (1661) — founding modern chemistry; and Isaac Newton's Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica (1687) — the laws of motion and universal gravitation, the single most influential scientific work ever published. Later works include Carl Linnaeus's Systema Naturae (1735) — the taxonomy of all living things. This corpus records the birth of the scientific worldview that defines modernity.
